analysis.title: What past investment booms can teach us about AI
key_insights: The biggest mistake in major investment booms is often underestimating duration, rather than focusing too narrowly on whether revenues can immediately justify investment.

Railways, electrification and China's industrial build-out each drew doubts about overinvestment, slow monetisation or excess capacity well before the cycle ended. Capital Group argues AI is facing the same ROI scepticism.
Capital Group frames AI as an S-curve investment cycle: adoption starts slowly, accelerates as use cases expand, then matures. Portfolio manager Nick Grace says the hard question is duration.

Equity valuations are part of the AI debate but are not unusually elevated across the market. The more immediate question is whether demand and monetisation can expand enough to support the build-out.

Five recurring boom patterns: demand broadens over time, ROI questions never disappear, volatility accompanies the opportunity, duration matters more than investors expect, and value shifts as bottlenecks move.

Question 1, demand: investors should check whether AI usage is broadening beyond early adopters, whether new use cases are emerging across industries, and whether demand is shifting from training and experimentation toward inference and live deployment.

Question 2, returns: AI can be adopted quickly while financial benefits stay unevenly distributed across companies, sectors and time. Broadening evidence of productivity and monetisation would make near-term ROI concerns look like a feature of the cycle.

Question 3, volatility: winning stocks in China compounded roughly 8-10 times with wicked volatility along the way. Volatility alone does not invalidate the structural AI opportunity unless adoption, investment and constraints weaken together.

Question 4, duration: in China, valuation was not a useful guidepost, and the cycle ended when supply balanced the market, much later than expected. Valuation still matters, but investors should also monitor adoption breadth, new demand sources, constraint movement and supply catch-up.

Question 5, supply constraints: value moves through the stack. For AI the focus has broadened from compute and chips to memory, networking, circuit boards, cooling, power, grids, copper, land and water, and financing.
Copper is the example of a bottleneck migrating outside tech. AI demand adds to electrification and grid demand, and long development timelines limit supply response.
If one constraint eases only for another to emerge, the build-out may have further to run. If supply catches up across several parts of the value chain, the cycle may be maturing.

The analogy has three limits: AI models can improve faster than earlier infrastructure cycles, AI model economics have no clean historical analogue, and markets may price bottlenecks faster than before, compressing some opportunities.

Economist Bobby Esnard notes that technology cycles and financial cycles can coincide with spillover. Financial cycles are vulnerable to liquidity, confidence, leverage and earnings disappointment even when valuations are not unusually high.
Capital Group says the opportunity set may broaden beyond today's largest technology companies as bottlenecks move into memory, networking, cooling, power and materials.
Signposts to watch: breadth of adoption, productivity and monetisation, movement of bottlenecks, supply response, and financial conditions and confidence.

sector_views.rationale: Early AI leadership was in compute, but value is expected to migrate to memory, networking, cooling and other parts of the stack. The note says the opportunity set may broaden beyond today's largest technology companies.

AI infrastructure adds to demand from electrification and grid investment, while long development timelines and supply constraints limit how fast production can respond. The note presents this as a bottleneck that could carry value.

risk_factors: Revenues may fail to keep pace with AI investment.
Competition and regulation could change the outcome.
Capital intensity and uncertain model economics.
Supply catching up with demand across several parts of the value chain would signal a maturing cycle.
Financial cycle fragility from liquidity, confidence, leverage and earnings disappointment, even if the technology cycle continues.
AI models can improve faster than earlier infrastructure, and markets may price bottlenecks faster, which could compress some opportunities.
Productivity gains staying confined to a narrow set of applications would make the ROI debate harder.

tension_points.bull_case: Past booms in railways, electrification and China's industrialisation were all doubted on ROI but ran longer than expected. Demand is still broadening and supply constraints keep moving through the stack.
tension_points.bear_case: Revenues may fail to keep pace with investment. Productivity gains confined to a narrow set of applications, and a financial cycle weakened by liquidity, confidence, leverage or earnings disappointment, would make the debate harder.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Adoption, investment and constraints weakening at the same time, or supply catching up with demand across several parts of the value chain.

theme_stances.key_argument: The larger mistake in booms is often underestimating how long demand can continue and how monetisation can develop.
theme_stances.evidence: the larger mistake is often underestimating how long demand can continue

theme_stances.key_argument: Value moves from compute into memory, networking, cooling, power, grids and materials as constraints shift.
theme_stances.evidence: bottlenecks are useful because they can indicate both where value may migrate
